🔸Monitor patient’s comfort and sweating response.

content:

🔺 RAKTHA MOKSHANAM / BLOOD LETTING THERAPY

📌DEFINITION

Raktamokṣaṇam is one of the Pañcakarma procedures in Ayurveda aimed at eliminating vitiated blood (doṣha-duṣhita rakta) from the body to cure blood-borne and Pitta-dominant disorders. It is a shodhana (purificatory) therapy.

📌DRUGS USED

🔸Jalaukā (leech)
🔸Alabu (bitter gourd shell)
🔸Śṛṅga (horn)
🔸Sirāvyadha (venesection instruments)
🔸Prachchanna (lancet, scalpel)


📌PROCEDURE

1. Purvakarma (pre-procedure):

🔸Examination of patient, selection of method (jalaukā, sirāvyadha, alabu, śṛṅga, prachchanna).
🔸Preparation of patient and area.

2. Pradhanakarma (main procedure)

🔸Application of the chosen method:
🔸Jalaukā (leech application): Leech is applied to the affected site.
🔸Sirāvyadha (venesection): Controlled incision in vein to let out blood.
🔸Alabu/Śṛṅga/Prachchanna: Localized bloodletting techniques.

3. Paschatkarma (post-procedure)

🔸Removal of leech/incision closure.
🔸Dressing, applying healing drugs, dietary advice, observation.

📌INDICATED DISEASES

🔸Vatarakta

🔸Arbuda
🔸Kushta
🔸Vidradhi
🔸Pidaka
🔸Shvitra
🔸Gridhrasi (in severe cases)
🔸Rakta-pitta
🔸Visha roga

📌MUST BE AVOIDED IN

🔸Bala (children)
🔸Vriddha (elderly)
🔸Stri (pregnant women, menstruating women)
🔸Alpa-rakta (anemia, low blood volume)
🔸Pandu roga (anemia)

🔸Atisara (diarrhea, dysentery)
🔸Kshata kshina (injury, debility)

📌PRECAUTIONS IN TREATMENT

🔸Patient should be examined for Bala (strength), Rakta mātra (blood volume), and Roga bala.
🔸Perform in aseptic conditions.
🔸Avoid excessive bloodletting to prevent shock, murcha (fainting), bala kshaya (weakness).
🔸Always keep stambhana (hemostatic drugs) ready.
🔸Post-therapy care: light diet, rest, avoiding exertion, spicy food, alcohol.

(Symptoms)

(Ref: Charaka Chikitsa 7/26–27; Sushruta Nidana 5/18)
*Śveta–rakta varna mandala (white patches with reddish border, like a lotus)
*Daha (burning sensation)
*Rukṣhatā (roughness)
*Kandu (itching)
*Srava (discharge sometimes present)
*Raga-mandala prachura (numerous circular patches)


🔺GENERAL EXAMINATION

*Built and nourishment: May vary; moderate to poor in chronic cases
*Skin: Presence of erythematous (reddish) patches with whitish scaly borders resembling lotus petals
*Itching: Mild to moderate pruritus
*Discoloration: Reddish or coppery with white scaling
*Lesion distribution: Commonly seen over trunk, limbs, and back
*Temperature: Usually normal
*Pulse & BP: Normal unless secondary infection or systemic disease present
*Associated findings: Possible mild burning or dryness over affected skin

🔺 SYSTEMIC EXAMINATION

1. Integumentary system:
*Circular, erythematous, or hypopigmented plaques with white scales
*Borders are well-defined with central clearing sometimes
2. Lymphatic system:
*Regional lymph node enlargement in chronic or infected cases
3. Nervous system:
*Usually normal (helps differentiate from leprosy)
4. Other systems (CVS, RS, GIT, CNS):
*No specific abnormalities unless associated systemic disease

🔺LABORATORY INVESTIGATIONS

1. Complete Blood Count (CBC): Usually normal, mild eosinophilia possible
2. Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR): May be mildly raised
3. Skin scraping for KOH test: To rule out fungal infection
   4.Skin biopsy: Shows epidermal hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, acanthosis (diagnostic for psoriasis)
5. Liver & renal function tests: To assess systemic involvement before therapy
6. Serological tests: ANA or HLA-Cw6 (if autoimmune suspicion)

*Tīvra vātabheda in śira
*Akasmāt patana (sudden falling / collapse) – key feature
*Aṅgānaṁ saṅkoca & prakampa (stiffening, tremors)
*Hṛllāsa, mūrcchā
*Vaktra–pādādi kampa

*Temperature
*Pulse rate (tachycardia / bradycardia)

*Hydration status: Dry mucosa, poor skin turgor, sunken eyes

*Nutritional status

*Higher mental functions

*Evidence of respiratory compromise

*Heart rate, rhythm

*Signs of shock
